# New renderings — odyssey-019 (4.538–640)

New house renderings introduced in this part, for copying into `conventions.md`'s table on
publication.

| Greek | `l` | `i` | avoided on purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| θέσφατόν ἐστι (561) | "it is god-declared" | "it is decreed" | "it is fated" (blurs it with the separate μοῖρα/πότμος word-family already used elsewhere in this part), "it is ordained" (loses the θεός root) |
| Ἠλύσιον πεδίον καὶ πείρατα γαίης (563) | "the Elysian plain and the ends of the earth" | "the Elysian plain, at the ends of the earth" | "Elysium" alone (drops πεδίον "plain"), "the edges of the world" (πείρατα is properly "limits, bounds", kept literal); the place is named only this once in the whole poem |
| θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ (548) | "manly spirit" | "proud spirit" | "manly heart" (θυμός is kept "spirit" throughout, reserving "heart" for ἦτορ/κραδίη), "overbearing spirit" (too negative a reading of ἀγήνωρ here) |
| τεληέσσας ἑκατόμβας (582) | "complete hecatombs" | "complete hecatombs" | "perfect", "unblemished" (both true to τέλος but drift from the literal "brought to completion"), "full hecatombs" (risks confusion with a literal headcount) |
| ἄσβεστον κλέος (584) | "fame unquenchable" | "fame that would never go out" | "undying fame" (that register is reserved for ἄφθιτον-type words, not used in this part), "imperishable renown" (too Latinate), "everlasting fame" (loses the fire-image in ἀ- + σβέννυμι) |
| ἤματα πάντα (592) | "all your days" | "for all your days" | "forever" (loses the concrete "days"), "all your life long" (too free) |
| δίφρον ἐύξοον (590) | "a well-polished car" | "a well-polished chariot" | "a well-planed chariot-board" (too technical), "a smooth car" (loses the craftsmanship sense of ξέω "plane, polish") |
| κρητῆρα τετυγμένον (615) / τετυγμένος generally | "a wrought mixing-bowl" | "a well-wrought mixing-bowl" | "a fashioned bowl" (flat), "a finely made bowl" (loses the link to τεύχω, the verb behind Homeric craftsmanship-formulas generally) |
| ἔργον Ἡφαίστοιο (617) | "the work of Hephaestus" | "the work of Hephaestus" | "Hephaestus's handiwork", "made by Hephaestus" (both lose the fixed formulaic shape of the phrase, a standing mark of the finest divine craftsmanship) |
| χειρί τέ μιν κατέρεξεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν (610, gesture-and-address formula) | "and stroked him with his hand, and spoke a word, and called him by name:" | "and stroked him with his hand, and spoke, calling him by name:" | "patted", "caressed" alone for κατέρεξεν (kept as "stroked" to distinguish from the firmer hand-clasp of the already-fixed ἔν τ’ ἄρα οἱ φῦ χειρί formula); the tail ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε(ν) keeps the wording already fixed for that formula's own closing words |
| Πύλῳ ἠγαθέῃ (599) | "holy Pylos" | "holy Pylos" | "very holy" (over-translates the intensive), "sacred Pylos" (risks confusion with the distinct, already-fixed "sandy Pylos" for a different epithet of the same city) |
| εὐρύχορον (635, of Elis) | "of wide dancing-grounds" | "spacious" | "of wide streets" (χορός is a dancing-place, not a street), "broad-lands" |
| ταλαεργοὶ ἡμίονοι (636) | "labour-enduring mules" | "labour-enduring... mules" | "hard-working" (loses the τλῆναι root, already used for "enduring-minded" ταλασίφρων), "toiling mules" |

## Judgment calls not producing a new table row

- **Quotation-mark scheme.** The still-open Proteus speech from odyssey-018 (opened 4.492, deliberately
  left unclosed at 4.537) is closed by the narrator's tag ὣς ἔφατ’ at 4.538; since its actual last
  words stand in the previous, already-published part, no closing ” character is added anywhere in
  this part for it — the tag itself carries the closure. A short narrative bridge (539–542) leads into
  a *distinct* fourth speech of Proteus's (543–547, ὣς ἔφατ’ at 538 and again at 548 close two
  different speeches, not one long one), opening its own fresh “ ” pair. Menelaus's own recalled
  question about "the third man" (551–553) takes the established single ‘ ’ pair, nested in his still
  unclosed outer narration to Telemachus (opened 4.333). Proteus's fifth and last speech in the poem
  (555–569) gets its own fresh “ ” pair, closing before his exit-formula ὣς εἰπὼν (570, distinct from
  ὣς ἔφατ’, a participle agreeing with ἐδύσετο rather than a narrator's tag). Menelaus's very long outer
  speech to Telemachus, opened at 4.333 (many parts before this one) and never touched again until now,
  is closed at the end of 592 (before the narrator-frame line τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος..., 593); its opening
  “ character accordingly does not appear anywhere in this file, so the part's overall “ ” count is one
  closing mark short of matching opens — this is expected and correct. Telemachus's reply (594–608),
  Menelaus's second reply (611–619), and Noemon's question (632–637) each get an ordinary fresh “ ” pair,
  opening and closing within this part.
- **μιν = Aegisthus at 546.** Left unnamed in the Greek (understood from the immediately preceding
  speech, 4.524–537, in the previous part); the note at that unit makes the referent explicit rather
  than leaving "him" ambiguous in English, where the antecedent is far less recoverable than in Greek.
- **ὑπὸ δ’ ἡμίονοι ταλαεργοί (636).** ὑπό is read in its sense "begotten under, born of" (the mules as
  offspring of the mares just named), not as a separate locative "and underneath [there were] mules";
  the note explains the breeding idiom rather than leaving a bare, opaque "under."
- **λωτός (603).** Read as the fodder-plant sense (a clover or trefoil grazed by horses), the ordinary
  Homeric sense of the word in a pastoral catalogue context, and kept apart in the note from any
  unrelated plant of the same name that may appear elsewhere in the poem, without asserting anything
  about a part this draft cannot show.
- **κατήλθομεν vs. κατήλυθον (573).** The Murray text here differs by one letter from the otherwise
  identical formula already shipped at 4.428–430 (odyssey-017); read as mere metrical variants of the
  same verb (κατέρχομαι), not a distinct sense, so the already-shipped English for the repeated second
  and third lines is reused unchanged, and only the first line's translation is freshly composed.
- **αἰγίβοτος, καὶ μᾶλλον ἐπήρατος ἱπποβότοιο (606).** Read with an understood copula and Ἰθάκη carried
  over as subject from the line before (ellipsis of both verb and subject, common in rapid Homeric
  description), rather than supplying any other subject.
